neighbours.label: two transliterated classics of Asian philosophy: the Tao Te Ching (Daodejing) and the three gunas of Hindu philosophy (sattva, rajas, tamas); other Daoist, Confucian and Buddhist names (Zhuangzi, Confucius, Laozi alone, Vajrayana) stay low
fire: She reads a chapter of the Tao Te Ching each morning.
The translator spent ten years on the Daodejing.
In Samkhya, the gunas are sattva, rajas and tamas.
Too much tamas, the teacher said, makes the mind dull.
A new edition of the Tao Te Ching came out in March.
Rajas is the guna of restless activity.
Our book club argued about the Tao Te Ching for hours.
Sattva is described as the guna of clarity.
quiet: She reads a chapter of the Analects each morning.
The translator spent ten years on the Zhuangzi.
In Buddhism, the three marks are impermanence, suffering and non-self.
Too much worry, the teacher said, makes the mind dull.
A new edition of the Bhagavad Gita came out in March.
Karma is the law of cause and effect.
Our book club argued about Confucius for hours.
Nirvana is described as the end of craving.
